course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.

themes.title: Interactions of humans with the environment
themes.question: How did geography, crops, resources, or disease shape choices?
themes.example: Andean terraces made steep slopes more usable for farming.

themes.title: Social interactions and organization
themes.question: Who had status, opportunities, or obligations?

themes.title: Political systems and governance
themes.question: How did rulers gain authority and administer territory?
themes.example: Song officials carried imperial decisions into local government.

themes.title: Economic systems

themes.example: Mali drew revenue from commerce through its territory.

themes.title: Cultural developments and interactions

themes.question: What techniques or tools changed what people could do?

lesson.title: Continuity and Change from 1450 to 1750
lesson.summary: What changed and what stayed the same as sea routes connected the world from 1450 to 1750.
learningGoals: Explain the continuities and changes in economic systems, labor, and trade from 1450 to 1750.
Support a claim about continuity and change with specific evidence.
lesson.bigIdea: Ocean voyages created the first global networks and transformed the Atlantic world, while much of Asia's economic power and many older trade patterns continued.
lesson.context: Continuity and change is an AP reasoning process. A strong answer names what changed, what stayed the same, and why.

sections.title: What changed

blocks.text: For the first time, sea routes linked every inhabited continent. The Columbian Exchange transformed diets and environments, and American silver created a global economy centered on Chinese demand.
The Atlantic world changed most. European empires, epidemic disease, and the forced migration of millions of Africans produced new societies in the Americas.

sections.takeaway: Global connection and the creation of Atlantic societies were the period's major changes.

sections.title: What continued

blocks.text: Asian merchants still carried most Indian Ocean trade. Chinese and Indian manufactured goods remained in demand worldwide, and land-based empires such as the Ottomans, Mughals, and Qing remained powerful.
Coerced labor also continued, though in new forms. Older systems of slavery and serfdom persisted while Atlantic chattel slavery expanded.

blocks.title: Cause and effect
blocks.text: Because Asian states were strong and Asian goods were valuable, Europeans had to join existing trade networks rather than replace them.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Do not claim Europeans dominated the world by 1750. Their power was greatest in the Americas and at sea, not in Asia's interior.

sections.takeaway: European expansion added to, rather than replaced, many older patterns.

connections.title: Toward industrialization
connections.body: Atlantic trade and profits from colonies contributed to the economic changes that led to industrialization in Britain after 1750, studied in Unit 5.
connections.transferQuestion: How might Atlantic trade have contributed to later economic change in Britain?
connections.feedback: Name a specific good or profit and explain its role.
